atoms.title: The neuron doctrine
atoms.summary: The nervous system is built from discrete cells — neurons — that are not continuous with one another, but signal across gaps.

depths.eli5: Your brain is made of cells. A long time ago, people argued about whether those cells were all joined into one big continuous mesh (like a fishing net with no gaps) or were separate little units. The neuron doctrine is the winning answer: the brain is built from separate cells called neurons, each its own closed bag with its own outer skin (its membrane). They are not fused together — they sit next to each other and pass signals across tiny gaps, the way people pass notes hand to hand instead of being wired into one circuit. A 'neuron' is just the name for one of these signaling cells.
depths.core: The older 'reticular theory' held that the nervous system was one continuous web of fused fibers. Using tissue stained by the Golgi method (a silver stain that randomly blackens a few whole cells so their full shape stands out), Santiago Ramón y Cajal argued the opposite: neurons are individual cells, each bounded by its own membrane (the cell's outer skin). The doctrine has four claims: (1) the neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system; (2) neurons are discrete cells, not physically fused; (3) within a neuron, signals normally flow one direction — from the dendrites (input branches) and soma (cell body) toward the axon (the output cable) and its terminals (the output tips); and (4) connections are specific and orderly, not random. This one-way-flow claim is called 'dynamic polarization.'
depths.deep: Cajal could not see the synaptic cleft (the gap between two neurons) directly — it is about 20 nanometers wide, far smaller than a light microscope can resolve (a nanometer is a billionth of a meter; visible light can only resolve features a few hundred nanometers across). So the doctrine was an inference from the shape of stained cells and the direction in which growing nerve tips (growth cones) extended, not a direct observation. It was only confirmed directly in the 1950s by the electron microscope, which uses electrons instead of light and can resolve such gaps. The dynamic-polarization principle — that signals run one way — is what makes a brain a computing device (with inputs, processing, and outputs) rather than a passive wire that conducts in any direction.

atoms.note: Cajal vs Golgi: they shared the 1906 Nobel Prize while still disagreeing — Golgi's own staining method, used by Cajal, is what defeated Golgi's reticular theory.

atoms.title: Neuron structure & compartments
atoms.summary: A neuron is organized into dendrites (input), soma (integration), axon (transmission), and terminals (output), each with distinct molecular machinery.

depths.eli5: Picture a neuron as a tree with a long trunk. The leafy branches at the top (called dendrites) collect incoming messages from other neurons. Those messages flow down to the main body of the cell (the soma, just a fancy word for the cell body, where the nucleus lives). If enough messages arrive, the neuron fires a signal that shoots down the long trunk (the axon — a thin cable that can be very long, up to about a meter in your leg) all the way to the tips at the far end (the terminals), where it hands the message to the next neuron. Input at the top, output at the bottom.
depths.core: A neuron is divided into compartments, each with a different job. Dendrites receive synaptic inputs (signals arriving from other neurons at junctions called synapses) and funnel them toward the soma (cell body). The axon hillock — the spot where the axon leaves the soma — is the decision point: it adds up the inputs and triggers a 'spike' (a nerve signal, formally an action potential) if they are strong enough. The axon, often wrapped in a fatty insulation called myelin, carries that all-or-none spike (it either fires fully or not at all) down to the presynaptic terminals, where chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) are released onto the next cell. Each compartment carries its own specialized set of ion channels (protein pores that let charged particles cross the membrane) and receptors (proteins that detect chemical messengers).
depths.deep: This compartmentalization is functional, not just anatomical. The axon initial segment (the very start of the axon) has the highest concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels (Na⁺ channels that open in response to voltage) in the whole cell, which is exactly why it is the spike-initiation zone. Dendrites are instead dominated by receptors and slower channels suited to gradually combining inputs. The nodes of Ranvier — small bare gaps along a myelinated axon — pack sodium channels so the spike can leap between them. The neuron's geometry (how its dendrites branch, how thick its axon is) directly shapes how it combines inputs, so shape is part of computation.

atoms.title: Ionic gradients & the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
atoms.summary: Active pumping maintains high K⁺ inside and high Na⁺ outside, storing the electrochemical energy every neural signal spends.

depths.eli5: Charged particles called ions float in and around every cell. Two of them matter here: sodium and potassium. A tiny machine in the cell's outer skin (a protein 'pump') constantly shoves sodium out of the cell and pulls potassium in. This leaves the inside and outside unequal — like separating two crowds — which stores energy, the same way pulling a slingshot back stores energy. Every nerve signal is that stored energy briefly being let go.
depths.core: An 'ion' is an atom carrying electric charge; sodium (written Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) are the key ones here, both positively charged. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase ('ATPase' means it burns ATP, the cell's energy currency) is a pump that swaps 3 sodium ions out of the cell for 2 potassium ions in, per ATP used — pushing each ion 'uphill' against its concentration gradient (from where it is scarce toward where it is already crowded). This builds an ionic imbalance: lots of potassium inside (~140 millimolar, a unit of concentration), lots of sodium outside (~145 mM). That imbalance is a stored reservoir of free energy (usable energy). Both the resting potential (the cell's steady idle voltage) and the action potential (the nerve spike) are controlled releases of this stored gradient.
depths.deep: The pump is electrogenic — each cycle moves a net of one positive charge out — so it adds a few millivolts (mV, thousandths of a volt) to the cell's voltage directly. But its main job is maintaining the concentration gradients that the Nernst and Goldman equations (covered next) use to compute the cell's voltage. Restoring these gradients after activity is a neuron's single largest energy cost, consuming roughly half the brain's entire energy budget. That is why neural signaling is, at bottom, an energy-management problem: the brain spends most of its fuel just keeping these batteries charged.

atoms.title: Nernst equilibrium potential
atoms.summary: For a single permeant ion, the membrane voltage at which diffusion and electrical drift exactly cancel.

depths.eli5: Charged particles (ions) naturally drift from where they are crowded to where they are sparse — that's just spreading out. But because ions carry electric charge, a voltage across the cell's skin can push them the other way. The Nernst potential is the exact voltage at which those two pushes — spreading-out versus electrical-pull — perfectly cancel, so the ion stops moving on net. Think of it as the 'tie score' voltage for one kind of ion.
depths.core: Suppose the cell membrane let only one ion, call it X, pass through. The voltage would settle at a value labeled E_X (the equilibrium or Nernst potential for X), where the concentration gradient pushing X one way is exactly balanced by the electrical gradient pushing it back, so no net current flows. In the equation, R is the gas constant, T is temperature, F is the Faraday constant, z is the ion's charge, and the ratio is the concentration outside over inside. At body temperature the lumped factor RT/F is about 26.7 mV, so a 10-fold concentration difference gives roughly ±61 mV (sign depending on the charge). For real neurons, potassium gives E_K ≈ −90 mV and sodium gives E_Na ≈ +60 mV.
depths.deep: The Nernst potential is an equilibrium statement — the voltage of zero net current for that ion — obtained by setting the ion's electrochemical potential equal on both sides of the membrane. It is the per-ion 'target voltage' that the real membrane gets pulled toward, more strongly for ions the membrane lets through more easily (higher conductance). This is the foundation for the Goldman equation (which blends several ions) and for the standard mental model of each channel type as a tiny battery (its E_X) wired in series with a resistor (its conductance).

atoms.note: 61 mV per tenfold concentration change (per 'decade'), for a singly charged ion at 37 °C, is the number worth memorizing.

atoms.title: Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz voltage equation
atoms.summary: The resting potential is a permeability-weighted blend of the individual ions' equilibrium potentials.

depths.eli5: A real cell membrane lets several kinds of ions through at once, not just one. So instead of a single tie-score voltage, the cell's actual voltage is a weighted average of all of them. The trick: an ion the membrane lets through easily gets a loud vote; an ion it barely lets through gets a quiet vote. Whichever ion passes most easily mostly decides the voltage.
depths.core: When several ions can cross, the membrane voltage V_m is not any single ion's Nernst potential but a weighted blend, where each ion is weighted by its permeability P (how easily that ion crosses the membrane). In the equation, [K]_o means potassium concentration outside, [K]_i inside, and so on for sodium (Na) and chloride (Cl). At rest the membrane lets potassium through far more easily than sodium, so V_m (about −70 mV) sits near E_K (−90 mV) but is nudged toward E_Na (+60 mV) by a small steady sodium leak. Chloride (Cl⁻) appears with its inside/outside concentrations flipped because it is negatively charged.
depths.deep: The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz (GHK) equation is derived under the 'constant-field assumption' (the electric field across the thin membrane is treated as uniform) and assumes each ion's flow is independent of the others. Its real power is dynamic: an action potential is essentially a brief surge in P_Na (sodium permeability) that drags V_m from near E_K up toward E_Na and back down. David Goldman (1943) and later Alan Hodgkin with Bernard Katz (1949) used it to turn the resting voltage from a mystery into something you can predict from a simple ratio of permeabilities.

atoms.note: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, so it 'votes' mostly for E_K; during a spike that permeability ratio briefly flips.

atoms.title: The resting membrane potential
atoms.summary: At rest a neuron sits near −70 mV, a dynamic steady state held by leak permeabilities and the pump, not a true equilibrium.

depths.eli5: Even when a neuron is doing nothing, the inside of the cell holds a steady voltage of about −70 millivolts (negative, meaning the inside is more negatively charged than the outside). 'Resting' doesn't mean frozen: ions are constantly leaking across the membrane, and a pump keeps working in the background to refill the battery and hold that voltage steady. The neuron pays energy just to stay idle.
depths.core: The resting membrane potential is the steady voltage at which the total electric current flowing across the membrane is zero (everything balances). Because the resting membrane is most permeable to potassium, V_m sits close to E_K (about −90 mV) but is dragged up to roughly −70 mV by a constant small sodium leak — exactly what the Goldman equation predicts. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump runs nonstop to replace the ions that leak through, so 'rest' is an actively maintained state, not a passive one.
depths.deep: Crucially this is a steady state, not thermodynamic equilibrium: K⁺ and Na⁺ are each off their own Nernst potentials, so each leaks down its gradient, and the pump spends ATP to keep the gradients constant. The cell pays energy continuously just to stay still. This standing potential is the operating point from which depolarizations are measured and the baseline the action potential springs from.

atoms.note: Resting V_m is a steady state, not a true equilibrium — ions constantly leak and the pump constantly restores them, burning ATP to stand still.

atoms.title: Passive membrane & the cable equation
atoms.summary: Below threshold a neuron behaves like a leaky cable, with characteristic time and length constants that smear and attenuate signals.

depths.eli5: Think of a nerve fiber as a leaky garden hose. If you inject a little voltage at one spot, it doesn't travel far cleanly — it spreads out, gets weaker, and smears over distance and time, because the 'hose' leaks. 'Passive' means we're looking at small signals too weak to trigger a full spike; on their own they just fade out unless the neuron actively boosts them.
depths.core: Below the firing threshold, a stretch of membrane behaves like a simple electrical circuit made of a resistor and a capacitor (an 'RC' circuit: a resistor resists current flow, a capacitor stores charge). Two numbers describe it. The membrane time constant τ_m = R_m·C_m (membrane resistance times capacitance) sets how quickly the voltage rises or falls when current is injected — how sluggish it is in time. The length constant λ = √(R_m/R_i) (R_i is the resistance of the fluid inside the fiber) sets how far a steady voltage spreads along the fiber before it shrinks to about 37% (the fraction 1/e ≈ 0.37) of its starting size. Together τ_m and λ define the window — in time and in space — over which a neuron adds up its incoming signals.
depths.deep: The cable equation is mathematically a diffusion equation with a leak term. It explains why inputs arriving far out on a dendrite are weakened before they reach the cell body, why thick myelinated axons (which have a large λ) carry passive signals farther and faster, and why an actively regenerating action potential is necessary at all — pure passive spread dies out within a few millimeters. You can think of τ_m and λ as the 'pixel size' of a neuron's integration: the finest resolution in time and space at which it combines its inputs.

atoms.title: Voltage-gated ion channels
atoms.summary: Membrane proteins whose pores open and close in response to voltage, providing the nonlinearity that makes spikes possible.

depths.eli5: These are tiny doors built into the cell's outer skin, made of protein. Each door can feel the voltage across the membrane and opens or shuts in response. When the voltage rises past a tipping point, sodium doors fly open, sodium rushes in, and that raises the voltage even more — which opens still more doors. This self-feeding chain reaction is exactly what makes a nerve signal explode into a full spike.
depths.core: A 'voltage-gated ion channel' is a protein pore that opens or closes depending on the membrane voltage. The sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) versions each contain a charged part called the voltage sensor (built from protein segments known as S4 helices) that physically moves when the membrane depolarizes (its voltage becomes less negative), pulling the pore open. The key is timing: sodium channels open fast and then 'inactivate' (auto-shut even though the voltage is still high), while potassium channels open more slowly and stay open. Fast sodium = quick positive feedback that drives the spike up; delayed potassium plus sodium shut-off = negative feedback that brings it back down. That timing difference is the engine of the action potential.
depths.deep: Each channel is selective — it lets the right ion through and blocks others — thanks to a narrow 'selectivity filter' lined with specific atoms (the potassium channel's filter, encoded by a signature stretch of protein, grips potassium ions after stripping off their water coat). 'Gating' is how the moving voltage sensor opens and closes the pore. Sodium-channel inactivation works by a separate 'ball-and-chain' plug that swings in to block the pore; this limits how long each spike lasts and creates a refractory period (a brief recovery time after a spike during which the cell can't easily fire again). That refractory period caps the maximum firing rate and gives spikes their all-or-none, one-direction-only character.

atoms.note: Fast Na⁺ opening = positive feedback; delayed K⁺ opening plus Na⁺ auto-shutdown = negative feedback. That timing IS the spike.

atoms.title: The action potential
atoms.summary: An all-or-none, self-regenerating voltage spike that carries digital signals down the axon without loss.

depths.eli5: An action potential is the actual nerve signal — a quick, sharp pulse of voltage. Here's the sequence: when the voltage at the neuron's trigger zone climbs past a tipping point (the threshold), a chain reaction lets sodium flood in, so the voltage shoots up steeply, then snaps back down. That pulse then travels along the axon like a row of dominoes falling, each patch knocking over the next, so the signal reaches the far end at full strength instead of fading.
depths.core: When the membrane depolarizes past threshold (its voltage rises to a tipping point), voltage-gated sodium channels open; sodium pouring in pushes the voltage higher, which opens still more sodium channels — runaway positive feedback that drives V_m (the membrane voltage) toward E_Na (sodium's equilibrium potential, about +60 mV). Then sodium channels inactivate (auto-shut) and slower potassium channels let potassium out, repolarizing the membrane (bringing it back down), often dipping briefly below the resting level (the after-hyperpolarization). The spike is 'all-or-none': its size carries no information — only whether and when it fires does.
depths.deep: Because the spike regenerates at every patch of membrane, it travels the whole axon without shrinking, solving the decay problem that limits passive cable spread. The refractory period (the brief recovery time set by sodium-channel inactivation) makes the signal travel one way only and turns the output into a series of discrete events in time (a 'point process'). In effect the action potential is the neuron's analog-to-digital converter: smoothly varying, graded input is gathered in the dendrites, and a clean digital train of spike times comes out the axon.

atoms.title: The Hodgkin–Huxley model
atoms.summary: A quantitative conductance-based model that reconstructs the action potential from voltage- and time-dependent gating variables.

depths.eli5: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley wrote down a set of equations describing how the tiny voltage-sensing doors in a nerve membrane open and close over time. When you let those equations run, they reproduce a real nerve spike almost perfectly. This was a landmark: the first time a living signal in the brain was fully predicted, in detail, by mathematics.
depths.core: Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) used the 'voltage clamp' — a technique that holds a cell at a fixed voltage so you can measure the current flowing — on the giant axon of a squid (large enough to insert electrodes). They modeled the membrane as a capacitor (charge store) wired in parallel with three conductances: one for sodium, one for potassium, and a constant 'leak.' Each conductance rises and falls according to gating variables — m and h control the sodium conductance, n controls the potassium conductance — and each variable obeys a simple rate law whose speed depends on voltage. Numerically solving the four linked equations on a computer reproduces the real spike's shape, its threshold, its refractoriness (recovery time), and how fast it travels.
depths.deep: The exponents in the equation (m³h for sodium, n⁴ for potassium) encode the idea that several independent gating 'particles' must all be in the open position at once for the channel to conduct — a strikingly accurate guess about the channels' multi-part structure, made decades before anyone could read a channel's genetic sequence. This model is the founding artifact of computational neuroscience: it proved a biological process could be captured exactly as a system of differential equations (equations describing rates of change). It earned the 1963 Nobel Prize and seeded every 'conductance-based' neuron simulator since.

atoms.note: The m³h and n⁴ exponents were inspired guesses about multiple gating particles — later vindicated by the four-domain / four-subunit architecture of the actual channels.

quiz.prompt: What do the gating variables m, h, and n represent in the Hodgkin–Huxley model?

quiz.prompt: Conceptually, why does the Na⁺ current term use m³h while the K⁺ term uses n⁴?
quiz.answer: Each represents the probability that several independent gating particles are simultaneously in the open/permissive state — three activating Na⁺ particles times one inactivation particle, and four activating K⁺ particles — matching the channels' multi-subunit structure.

atoms.title: Myelin & saltatory conduction
atoms.summary: Insulating myelin forces the spike to jump between nodes of Ranvier, vastly speeding conduction at low metabolic cost.

depths.eli5: Many axons are wrapped in a fatty insulating sleeve called myelin, with small bare gaps left along the way. Instead of crawling slowly along every inch of the fiber, the signal leaps from bare gap to bare gap — much faster, like a stone skipping across water instead of rolling along the bottom. 'Saltatory' just means 'jumping.'
depths.core: Helper cells called glia (oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord, Schwann cells in the body's peripheral nerves) wrap the axon in myelin. The myelin makes those wrapped stretches leak less current (higher resistance) and store less charge (lower capacitance). The voltage-gated sodium channels that regenerate the spike are bunched up only at the bare gaps — the nodes of Ranvier — between myelin segments. So the spike fires fresh at each node, then spreads quickly and passively along the insulated stretch (the internode) to the next node, appearing to jump, or 'saltate,' from node to node.
depths.deep: Myelin increases the length constant λ (how far passive voltage spreads) and lowers the membrane capacitance C_m, so the passive jump between nodes is both longer and faster, while active regeneration at the nodes keeps the signal from decaying. The payoff is conduction speeds up to about 120 meters per second in large myelinated fibers, versus roughly 1 m/s in bare ones — and far fewer sodium ions enter, so much less energy is spent pumping them back out. It is a joint win on both speed and energy. When myelin is damaged — as in multiple sclerosis, a disease that strips it — conduction slows or fails.

atoms.title: The chemical synapse
atoms.summary: At most synapses, a presynaptic spike triggers Ca²⁺-dependent neurotransmitter release that changes the postsynaptic cell's voltage.

depths.eli5: Where two neurons meet there's a tiny gap called a synapse. When a spike arrives at the end of the first neuron, it can't jump the gap electrically, so instead it squirts out chemical messengers. Those chemicals drift across the gap and land on the second neuron, nudging it either toward firing or away from firing. This is how most neurons talk to each other.
depths.core: When the spike reaches the axon terminal, it opens voltage-gated calcium (Ca²⁺) channels. Calcium rushing in triggers little membrane sacs called vesicles — each pre-filled with neurotransmitter (the chemical messenger) — to fuse with the cell's edge and dump their contents into the gap (a process called exocytosis). The transmitter drifts across the synaptic cleft (about 20 nanometers wide) and binds receptors on the receiving (postsynaptic) cell, opening ion channels there. This produces a small, graded postsynaptic potential — either excitatory (an EPSP, nudging toward firing) or inhibitory (an IPSP, nudging away). Transmission goes one way only and takes a short delay of about 0.5–1 millisecond.
depths.deep: Release is 'quantal': vesicles deliver fixed-size packets, so the receiving cell's response comes in whole-number multiples of one vesicle's effect (Bernard Katz's quantal hypothesis). Calcium is the trigger because the molecular fusion machinery (the SNARE proteins plus a calcium sensor called synaptotagmin) is built to detect calcium — which makes release rise very steeply (roughly with the fourth power) as calcium concentration climbs. So a chemical synapse is not a plain wire: it is a chemically controlled relay that can be strengthened or weakened (it is 'plastic') and can flip sign between excite and inhibit — making it the basic unit of both computation and learning.

atoms.note: Quantal release (Katz): the receiving cell's responses come in whole-number multiples of a single-vesicle 'quantum.'

quiz.answer: Ca²⁺; the arriving action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the presynaptic terminal.

quiz.prompt: What does it mean that synaptic transmission is 'quantal'?
quiz.answer: Neurotransmitter is released in discrete packets (vesicles), so the postsynaptic response is an integer multiple of the response to a single vesicle's 'quantum'.

atoms.title: Electrical synapses & gap junctions
atoms.summary: Gap junctions directly couple neurons electrically, giving fast, bidirectional, near-instant signal transfer.

depths.eli5: Not all neurons use chemical messengers. Some are joined by direct microscopic tunnels, so electric current flows straight from the inside of one cell into the next with no gap to cross. That makes the connection extremely fast — there's no chemistry to wait for.
depths.core: At an electrical synapse, matching half-channels (called connexons, built from proteins called connexins) on two neighboring cells line up and dock to form a gap junction: a continuous pore that lets ions and small molecules pass directly between the two cells' interiors (their cytoplasms). Current flows with essentially no delay and usually in both directions, so connected neurons change voltage almost in lockstep. That makes electrical synapses ideal for synchronizing whole groups of neurons and for fast escape reflexes where every fraction of a millisecond counts.
depths.deep: Compared with chemical synapses, electrical synapses trade flexibility for raw speed. They have no transmission delay, no easy way to invert the sign (so they can't readily inhibit), and limited ability to strengthen or weaken — but they excel at keeping cells in sync. Real networks often mix both kinds: gap junctions linking inhibitory interneurons help generate coordinated gamma-band brain rhythms, while chemical synapses do most of the heavy computational work.

quiz.prompt: Why are electrical synapses well suited to generating synchronized network oscillations?
quiz.answer: Their fast, bidirectional coupling makes connected neurons depolarize nearly simultaneously, promoting coherent population rhythms.

atoms.title: Neurotransmitters & receptor types
atoms.summary: Transmitters act through fast ionotropic (channel) receptors and slow metabotropic (G-protein) receptors, setting a synapse's speed and sign.

depths.eli5: Neurotransmitters are the chemical messages neurons send. The receiving cell has 'locks' (receptors) that only certain messengers fit. Some locks, when opened, instantly swing a door open and let charged particles flood in. Other locks instead kick off a slower chain of events inside the cell. So the same gap can carry fast or slow signals depending on which lock the message lands on.
depths.core: Common neurotransmitters include glutamate (the main 'go' / excitatory signal), GABA and glycine (the main 'stop' / inhibitory signals), and modulators such as acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine that adjust overall tone. Receptors come in two families. Ionotropic receptors (examples: AMPA, NMDA, GABA_A) are 'ligand-gated' channels — the messenger ('ligand') binds and the channel itself pops open, giving a response within milliseconds. Metabotropic receptors (examples: mGluR, and most dopamine and serotonin receptors) don't open a channel directly; they activate internal relay proteins (G proteins) and 'second messengers' inside the cell, producing slower effects lasting hundreds of milliseconds to minutes.
depths.deep: A crucial point: the synapse's sign (excite vs inhibit) is set by the receptor on the receiving cell, not by the transmitter alone. Glutamate opens channels that let in positive ions (excitatory); GABA acting on GABA_A receptors opens chloride channels (usually inhibitory). The NMDA receptor is special — it is gated by both the chemical AND the voltage (a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺, plugs it until the cell is depolarized). That makes it a molecular 'coincidence detector' that fires only when input and activity happen together — the linchpin of Hebbian learning (covered later). The slow, metabotropic pathway is the basis of neuromodulation, which retunes whole circuits at once.

atoms.note: The receptor, not the transmitter, sets a synapse's sign and speed — the same molecule can excite at one receptor and inhibit at another.

quiz.prompt: What is the key functional difference between ionotropic and metabotropic receptors?
quiz.answer: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels producing fast (millisecond) responses; metabotropic receptors act through G proteins and second messengers, giving slower, longer-lasting effects.

quiz.prompt: Why is the NMDA receptor described as a 'coincidence detector'?
quiz.answer: It opens only when glutamate is bound AND the postsynaptic cell is depolarized enough to expel its Mg²⁺ block, so it signals the coincidence of presynaptic input and postsynaptic activity — the substrate for Hebbian learning.

atoms.title: Synaptic integration & spatiotemporal summation
atoms.summary: A neuron decides to fire by summing many graded EPSPs and IPSPs across its dendrites in space and time.

depths.eli5: A neuron is constantly getting little nudges from thousands of other neurons — some pushing it toward firing, some pulling it back. It doesn't react to any single nudge; it adds them all up. If the running total at the trigger zone is big enough, the neuron fires a spike. That adding-up process is called synaptic integration.
depths.core: Each synapse produces only a small graded potential (a tiny voltage bump or dip); the neuron sums many of them. Spatial summation adds inputs arriving at different places on the cell at the same moment. Temporal summation adds inputs arriving at nearly the same place in quick succession — how 'quick' is set by the membrane time constant τ_m. Excitatory (toward-firing) and inhibitory (away-from-firing) inputs combine, and the net voltage at the axon initial segment (the trigger zone) decides whether the firing threshold is reached. One synapse alone is almost always far too weak to fire the cell.
depths.deep: This summation is not a plain straight-line addition. Dendrites have their own active machinery (such as local NMDA-receptor 'spikes' and other voltage-sensitive channels) that let a single dendritic branch behave like a mini-processor doing AND-like logic (fire only if several inputs land together). So one neuron can act like a small multi-layer network rather than a single adding point. Inhibition placed near the cell body can cancel ('shunt') excitation arriving from farther out (shunting inhibition). This is exactly where the cell's physical shape turns into computation.

quiz.prompt: How can dendritic nonlinearities make a single neuron compute more than a simple weighted sum?
quiz.answer: Local active conductances (e.g., NMDA spikes) let individual dendritic branches perform AND-like or thresholding operations before the soma, so the cell behaves like a small multilayer network rather than one linear summing point.

atoms.title: Long-term potentiation & depression
atoms.summary: Synaptic strength can be persistently increased (LTP) or decreased (LTD) by patterns of activity — the cellular basis of memory.

depths.eli5: Synapses (the junctions between neurons) have an adjustable strength, like a volume dial. Use a connection a lot in the right pattern and the dial turns up and stays up — that lasting strengthening is called long-term potentiation, LTP. Use it the wrong way and the dial turns down — long-term depression, LTD. The brain learns and remembers largely by adjusting these dials, and the changes can last for years.
depths.core: At many glutamate-using ('glutamatergic') synapses, strong or precisely coincident activity strongly activates NMDA receptors, letting calcium (Ca²⁺) into the receiving cell's dendritic spine (a tiny bump where a synapse sits). That calcium triggers more AMPA receptors (the fast-acting glutamate receptors) to be inserted into the membrane, so the synapse responds more strongly from then on — that is LTP. A weaker but longer-lasting calcium signal does the opposite: it removes AMPA receptors, weakening the synapse — that is LTD. Both can last from hours to a lifetime, which is exactly what a lasting memory needs.
depths.deep: Calcium acts as a decision switch through its size and timing: a large, fast calcium rise activates an enzyme called CaMKII and produces LTP, while a modest, sustained rise activates opposing enzymes (phosphatases) and produces LTD (the basis of a 'sliding threshold' idea known as the BCM rule). Early LTP just shuffles existing receptors around; late, long-lasting LTP requires the cell to switch on genes and build new proteins, which get 'captured' at the synapses that were recently active (the synaptic tagging and capture idea). In short, LTP and LTD are the real-synapse machinery behind 'Hebbian learning.'

atoms.note: Calcium is the decision variable: a big fast rise → LTP (strengthen); a small sustained rise → LTD (weaken).

quiz.answer: A large, fast NMDA-mediated Ca²⁺ rise drives LTP (more AMPA receptors); a smaller, sustained Ca²⁺ rise drives LTD (fewer AMPA receptors).

quiz.prompt: Why does late-phase LTP, but not early LTP, require new protein synthesis?
quiz.answer: Early LTP is implemented by trafficking existing AMPA receptors; making the change persist for many hours requires gene transcription and new proteins, captured at tagged active synapses.

atoms.title: Hebbian learning
atoms.summary: "Neurons that fire together wire together" — correlated pre- and postsynaptic activity strengthens their connection.

depths.eli5: Here's the brain's simplest learning rule, in plain words: if neuron A keeps helping neuron B fire, the connection from A to B gets stronger. The catchphrase is 'neurons that fire together, wire together.' Connections that reliably help cause activity get reinforced, so the brain gradually wires up the patterns it keeps seeing.
depths.core: Donald Hebb's 1949 idea: when neuron A repeatedly takes part in firing neuron B, the synapse (connection) from A to B is strengthened. Written as a formula, the change in connection strength (the 'weight,' w) is proportional to the product of the input activity x and the output activity y: Δw ∝ x·y, so the weight grows only when both are active together. Two features matter: it's local (each synapse uses only the signals available right at it) and it's correlation-based (it responds to inputs and outputs happening together). This is the conceptual root of 'unsupervised' learning in artificial neural networks — learning structure from data with no answer key.
depths.deep: Pure Hebbian strengthening is unstable: because strong synapses fire the cell more, which strengthens them further, weights run away to infinity. Real systems fix this by adding normalization (keeping the total connection strength bounded) or a 'sliding threshold' (the BCM rule) that subtracts an activity-dependent term, allowing connections to weaken as well as strengthen and producing useful selectivity — like neurons that prefer one eye (ocular dominance) or one edge orientation. The cleanest biological implementation is NMDA-receptor-dependent LTP, which strengthens a synapse only when input and output activity coincide — exactly Hebb's condition.

atoms.note: 'Fire together, wire together' is catchy but incomplete — without a weakening term or normalization, Hebbian weights blow up.

quiz.prompt: State Hebb's rule in one line and write its simplest mathematical form.
quiz.answer: If A helps fire B, strengthen A→B; the weight change is proportional to the product of pre- and postsynaptic activity, Δw ∝ x·y.

quiz.prompt: Why must a learning rule add depression or normalization to a pure Hebbian term?
quiz.answer: Pure Hebbian strengthening is positive-feedback and makes weights grow without bound; a depression term or normalization (e.g., BCM's sliding threshold) stabilizes weights and produces input selectivity.

atoms.title: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity
atoms.summary: The sign and size of synaptic change depend on the millisecond timing between pre- and postsynaptic spikes.

depths.eli5: This is Hebbian learning sharpened to the millisecond. Whether a connection grows stronger or weaker depends on the exact order of two spikes: if the input neuron fires just BEFORE the receiving neuron does, the link strengthens; if it fires just AFTER, the link weakens. The order — within a few thousandths of a second — decides which way the dial turns.
depths.core: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is a time-precise version of Hebbian learning. When the presynaptic (sending) spike comes a few milliseconds before the postsynaptic (receiving) spike, the synapse strengthens (LTP); when it comes after, the synapse weakens (LTD). Guo-qiang Bi and Mu-ming Poo (1998) measured the 'STDP window': the amount of strengthening or weakening falls off exponentially as the spike-time gap Δt (the difference between the two spike times) grows, with characteristic time scales of roughly 10–20 ms and essentially no effect once the gap exceeds about 40–100 ms.
depths.deep: The asymmetry of the window implements causal inference — figuring out what causes what. Inputs that help cause a spike (they arrive just before) are strengthened; inputs that arrive too late to have helped are weakened. So a neuron tuned by STDP comes to favor inputs that predict its own firing, and the network can learn ordered sequences and predictive relationships. Mechanistically STDP rides on NMDA-receptor coincidence detection plus the 'back-propagating action potential' — a copy of the output spike that travels backward into the dendrites to announce 'I just fired,' so each synapse can compare its input timing against the cell's output. STDP is a leading model for how networks self-organize with no external teacher.

atoms.note: Pre-before-post → strengthen (the input may have caused the spike); post-before-pre → weaken. The window is only tens of milliseconds wide.

atoms.title: Neural coding: rate vs temporal codes
atoms.summary: Information can be carried by how fast neurons fire (rate code) or by the precise timing of individual spikes (temporal code).

depths.eli5: Since every spike is the same size, a neuron can't shout 'louder.' So how does it say how strong something is? Two ways. It can fire more spikes per second (a 'rate code' — more spikes means a stronger signal). Or it can carry meaning in the exact timing and rhythm of its spikes (a 'temporal code' — when each spike lands matters). Both carry information, and the brain uses each in different places.
depths.core: A rate code represents a stimulus by the average firing rate (spikes per second) over some time window. It's robust to noise but slow, and it throws away the fine detail of individual spike times. A temporal code instead uses the precise timing — or the relative latency (which neuron fired first) — of spikes; it can pack more information into each spike and react faster. Real neurons often use both: a rate code for slowly changing signals, and timing (for example, the phase of a spike relative to an ongoing brain rhythm) for fast or relational information.
depths.deep: Which code is used is constrained by reliability and by what reads the signal downstream. Rate codes need integration time but tolerate jitter (slightly noisy spike times). Temporal codes are information-dense but demand precise, reliable spiking and timing-sensitive readers such as coincidence detectors (cells that fire only when inputs arrive together). Examples of timing-based codes include hippocampal 'theta phase precession' (a spike's phase within a rhythm shifts to encode position) and first-spike-latency codes (the first cell to fire signals the strongest input) — both show the brain exploiting timing when speed or capacity demand it.

atoms.title: Population & distributed coding
atoms.summary: Many noisy neurons together represent a variable more accurately than any single cell, often via overlapping tuning curves.

depths.eli5: Any single neuron is a noisy, unreliable guesser. But if you have a whole crowd of neurons, each tuned to prefer a slightly different thing, you can take a vote and the average comes out sharp and accurate — like polling many people instead of asking one. So meaning lives in the pattern of activity across many cells, not in any one cell by itself.
depths.core: Population coding represents a stimulus using the combined activity of many neurons, each with its own tuning curve — a graph showing which value it responds to most (its preferred direction, edge orientation, sound frequency, and so on). Because each cell's noise is largely its own, averaging across the population cancels that noise out. A simple readout like a 'population vector,' or a statistical best-guess method (maximum-likelihood decoding), can then recover the encoded value far more precisely than any single cell could. Spreading the code across many cells also makes it robust: losing a few neurons barely hurts.
depths.deep: Apostolos Georgopoulos's population-vector work showed the motor cortex encodes the direction of an arm movement as the vector sum of many cells' preferred directions, each weighted by how hard it is firing. More generally, how well you can decode a population depends on the structure of its correlated noise — noise patterns that look like the signal limit the information available, while noise patterns pointing in unrelated directions do not. Real brains use 'sparse, distributed' codes (a modest fraction of cells active for any item) that balance capacity, energy cost, and ease of decoding — which is why the brain uses neither single 'grandmother cells' (one cell per concept) nor fully dense codes.

atoms.note: The population vector: each neuron 'votes' along its preferred stimulus, weighted by its firing rate; the vector sum of all those votes is the estimate.

quiz.answer: Averaging across many cells with overlapping tuning curves cancels their independent noise, so the population estimate is far sharper than a single noisy neuron's.

atoms.title: Neural circuits: excitation, inhibition & motifs
atoms.summary: Neurons wire into recurring circuit motifs — feedforward and feedback inhibition, lateral inhibition, recurrence — that perform stereotyped computations.

depths.eli5: Neurons don't connect at random; they wire up in a handful of repeating little patterns, like reusable Lego shapes. Each pattern does a specific job — sharpening a signal, keeping the overall activity from going wild, or holding onto a piece of information. Build a brain out of these few building blocks and you get all its different functions.
depths.core: Circuits are assembled from a few recurring wiring patterns ('motifs'). Feedforward inhibition (an input excites a target and also, slightly later, an inhibitory cell that quiets that target) creates precise timing windows. Feedback (recurrent) inhibition (active cells switch on inhibitory neighbors that calm them) stabilizes and normalizes activity. Lateral inhibition (active cells suppress their neighbors) sharpens contrast. Recurrent excitation (cells that re-excite each other) can sustain activity to hold a memory or amplify a weak input. Keeping excitation and inhibition roughly matched — the 'E/I balance' — keeps a network sensitive and responsive instead of either silent or saturated (maxed out).
depths.deep: Inhibition is far more than an off switch. It can implement division (turning a signal down by a factor — gain control or 'normalization'), gate whether information passes, help generate rhythmic oscillations, and produce winner-take-all dynamics (one option suppresses the rest until a single winner remains). Tight E/I balance yields irregular, unsynchronized firing that is both energy-efficient and quick to respond, plausibly keeping the network near a 'critical point' (a finely poised regime, explored in a later atom). These motifs are the brain's reusable subroutines, appearing everywhere from the retina to the cortex.

quiz.answer: It sharpens contrast by having active neurons suppress their neighbors — classically seen in the retina (and other sensory maps), enhancing edges and boundaries.

atoms.title: Working memory & persistent activity
atoms.summary: Holding information in mind for seconds may be implemented by recurrent excitation that sustains activity after a stimulus is gone.

depths.eli5: Working memory is your mental scratchpad — the way you hold a phone number in mind for a few seconds while you dial. One way the brain does this: a group of neurons keeps firing on its own even after the thing you heard is gone, like an echo the brain deliberately keeps going so the information doesn't vanish.
depths.core: Working memory is the short-term, active holding and manipulation of information — the prefrontal cortex (the front of the brain) acting like a mental sketchpad. A classic mechanism is persistent neuronal activity: during the 'delay' part of a memory task (after the cue disappears, before you respond), certain prefrontal neurons keep firing for the remembered item even though nothing is on screen. Loops of recurrent excitation (neurons re-exciting each other), held in check by inhibition, settle into self-sustaining states called attractors that keep the memory alive. The catch: that same self-feeding activity is also what makes the memory easy to knock off course with a distraction.
depths.deep: Attractor-network models picture this as a stable 'bump' of activity in a recurrent network — a continuous attractor for analog quantities (like a remembered angle) or discrete attractors for distinct categories — tuned near a tipping point (a bifurcation) so a brief input can flip the state on or off. Newer evidence suggests information can also be stored 'activity-silent' — held in fleeting short-term synaptic changes rather than ongoing firing, and reawakened only when probed — so persistent firing may be just one of several mechanisms. Working memory is the bridge from circuit dynamics up to cognition, and many theories treat it as the gateway to conscious access.

atoms.note: Persistent delay-period firing in prefrontal cortex is the classic mechanism; 'activity-silent' synaptic traces are a newer, complementary one.

atoms.title: Sensory transduction
atoms.summary: Receptor cells convert physical stimuli — light, sound, pressure, chemicals — into graded electrical signals.

depths.eli5: Your senses are translators that turn things in the world into electricity the brain can read. The eye turns light into electrical signals, the ear turns sound vibrations into them, the skin turns pressure into them. The brain never touches light or sound directly — everything it knows arrives as voltage. That translation step is called sensory transduction.
depths.core: Each sense has its own special machinery that converts a stimulus into the opening or closing of ion channels (those protein pores again). In vision, light hits photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) and sets off a chemical relay chain (a 'G-protein cascade': the light-sensing pigment rhodopsin activates a relay protein, transducin, then an enzyme, PDE, which lowers a small signaling molecule called cGMP, which closes channels). In hearing, hair cells in the cochlea (the inner ear's coiled tube) have tiny hairs (stereocilia) that, when bent by sound vibrations, mechanically yank channels open. Touch and smell receptors open channels by force or by a molecule binding. In every case the output is a graded receptor potential — a voltage whose size tracks how strong the stimulus is.
depths.deep: The transduction step sets the sensitivity and 'dynamic range' (the span from faintest to strongest detectable) of each sense. Vision's multi-step chemical cascade provides enormous amplification — a single photon can produce a measurable electrical current — but takes time, so it is slow. Hearing's mechanical gating is direct and microsecond-fast, which is what lets you locate sounds by the tiny timing difference between your two ears. Built-in adaptation at the transduction step (often via calcium feedback) lets receptors keep working across a vast range of intensities, from a dim star to bright sunlight.

atoms.title: Receptive fields
atoms.summary: A sensory neuron responds only to stimuli in a specific region and pattern — its receptive field — built by circuit wiring.

depths.eli5: Each sensory neuron is picky. It has a favorite spot in the world (a particular patch of your visual field, say) and a favorite kind of pattern there. Show it the right thing in the right place and it fires hard; show it anything else and it stays quiet. That favorite spot-and-pattern is the neuron's 'receptive field.'
depths.core: A receptive field is the region of sensory space — plus the specific pattern within it — that makes a neuron respond. In vision, retinal ganglion cells and cells in the LGN (the lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay station between eye and cortex) have 'center-surround' fields: a small central spot that excites and a ring around it that inhibits (built by lateral inhibition), so the cell detects local contrast rather than uniform light. David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel showed that neurons in the primary visual cortex have oriented receptive fields — 'simple cells' fire best for an edge or bar at a particular angle and position, built by lining up several center-surround inputs in a row.
depths.deep: Receptive fields are effectively the brain's feature detectors. A center-surround field behaves like an edge/contrast filter (mathematically similar to a Laplacian operator); an oriented simple-cell field resembles a 'Gabor function,' which happens to be an efficient, sparse way to encode the statistics of natural images. The step from center-surround (spots) to oriented edges is the first rung of a processing hierarchy — and it is essentially the same operation that the first layers of a convolutional neural network learn to perform, one of the clearest links between brains and modern AI vision.

atoms.note: Hubel & Wiesel (1981 Nobel Prize): cortical simple cells are built by aligning several LGN center-surround inputs along an axis, which yields orientation tuning.

atoms.title: Hierarchical sensory processing
atoms.summary: Sensory systems build increasingly abstract representations through successive stages, each pooling simpler features into more complex ones.

depths.eli5: Vision is built up in stages, like an assembly line. The first stage sees tiny edges. The next combines edges into corners and textures. The next builds shapes. The last recognizes whole objects and faces. Each stage takes the pieces found by the stage before it and assembles bigger, more meaningful pieces.
depths.core: Along the brain's visual 'ventral stream' — a chain of areas labeled V1 → V2 → V4 → IT (inferotemporal cortex) — two things change at each step. Receptive fields get larger (each cell looks at more of the image), and what cells respond to gets more abstract: from oriented edges, to contours and textures, to object parts, to whole objects and faces. Higher stages also gain 'invariance' — they keep recognizing an object even when it shifts position or changes size. This same feedforward-and-pooling principle shows up across the senses and is the direct architectural inspiration for deep convolutional neural networks.
depths.deep: The hierarchy trades away fine spatial detail in exchange for abstraction and invariance. It does this by alternating two kinds of stages: selectivity-increasing stages (AND-like template matching — fire only for a specific combination) and invariance-increasing stages (OR-like pooling — fire if the feature appears anywhere nearby). That is the simple-cell/complex-cell idea, generalized up the chain. Importantly, the brain's hierarchy is not a one-way street: it has abundant feedback connections carrying context and expectations back down — which is exactly what 'predictive coding' models (a later atom) try to capture.

atoms.title: Motor control & the motor hierarchy
atoms.summary: Movement is produced by a hierarchy from cortical planning through spinal circuits to motor units, with feedback correction throughout.

depths.eli5: Moving your body is a team effort across levels. Up top, your brain decides the goal ('reach for the cup'). Lower down, the spinal cord runs the automatic reflexes and rhythmic patterns (like the leg cycle of walking). At the bottom, muscles do the actual pulling. And all the while, feedback flows back so the system can fix small errors as the movement happens.
depths.core: The 'final common path' is the motor unit: one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it controls. Force is graded two ways — by recruiting more motor units and by making them fire faster. Spinal circuits handle reflexes and house 'central pattern generators,' little oscillator circuits that produce rhythmic actions like walking without needing step-by-step commands from the brain. The motor and premotor cortex plan and choose movements; the cerebellum (a structure at the back of the brain) and basal ganglia (deep brain nuclei) fine-tune timing, coordination, and which action to take. Sensory feedback and the brain's own predictions ('forward models') correct the movement while it's still in progress.
depths.deep: Control theory (the math of steering systems) fits this well. The brain runs internal 'forward models' that predict the sensory consequences of its own motor commands. That prediction lets it correct movements quickly even though real sensory feedback is delayed, and it explains why self-generated sensations feel muted — you can't tickle yourself because your brain predicted (and discounted) your own touch. At the level of populations, motor cortex activity is well described by low-dimensional dynamics — a few combined patterns that evolve over time to generate the muscle commands — a 'dynamical systems' view that has largely replaced the older idea that each neuron simply codes one movement parameter.

atoms.title: Hippocampus & declarative memory
atoms.summary: The hippocampus is required to form new conscious (declarative) memories and supports spatial mapping via place cells.

depths.eli5: The hippocampus is a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that works like a 'save' button for new facts and events. If it's damaged, you can still recall your childhood and still learn physical skills, but you can't lay down new lasting memories of what just happened. It doubles as the brain's inner GPS, tracking where you are.
depths.core: The famous patient H.M., who had both hippocampi removed to treat epilepsy, could no longer form new declarative memories — the consciously recallable kind, covering episodic (specific events) and semantic (facts) memory — yet he kept his old memories and could still learn new motor skills. This showed the hippocampus is needed to encode new conscious memories but is not where they are permanently stored. The hippocampus also holds 'place cells' (discovered by John O'Keefe) that fire only when the animal is in a specific location, together forming a 'cognitive map'; nearby 'grid cells' in the entorhinal cortex lay down a coordinate-like grid.
depths.deep: The hippocampus rapidly binds the pieces of an experience into a single combined code, using two complementary tricks: 'pattern separation' in a region called the dentate gyrus (making similar experiences distinct so they don't blur) and 'pattern completion' in the recurrent network of region CA3 (letting a partial cue retrieve the whole memory). Both lean heavily on NMDA-receptor-dependent LTP. The same circuit 'replays' recent experience during brief bursts called sharp-wave ripples during rest and sleep — the proposed engine for copying memories into the neocortex. That place and grid cells live in the memory system hints the brain treats remembering as a kind of navigation through a represented space.

atoms.note: H.M. separates declarative (hippocampus-dependent) from procedural memory; O'Keefe and the Mosers (2014 Nobel Prize) found place and grid cells.

quiz.prompt: How do place cells and pattern separation/completion let the hippocampus store distinct episodes?

atoms.title: Systems consolidation
atoms.summary: Memories initially dependent on the hippocampus are gradually stabilized into distributed neocortical stores, especially during sleep.

depths.eli5: A brand-new memory is fragile at first and leans on the hippocampus. Over days to years it gets gradually copied into the broader cortex (the brain's outer sheet), until it can stand on its own without the hippocampus. Sleep is when a lot of that copying happens, which is part of why sleep helps you remember.
depths.core: Systems consolidation is the slow reorganization by which a memory stops depending on the hippocampus and ends up stored in widely distributed neocortical networks. The standard model: the hippocampus quickly binds an experience, then repeatedly reactivates ('replays') it — especially during slow-wave (deep, dreamless) sleep — gradually training cortical synapses until the cortical version of the memory can stand alone. This is a different process from synaptic consolidation, the faster (hours-long) stabilization of individual synapses by new protein synthesis covered in the LTP atom.
depths.deep: The proposed teaching signal is replay during sharp-wave ripples (those brief hippocampal bursts), timed to line up with cortical slow oscillations and thalamic 'sleep spindles.' In this 'complementary learning systems' view, the hippocampus is a fast learner that interleaves new memories gradually into a slow cortical learner, which prevents new learning from overwriting old (a failure mode called catastrophic interference). Consolidation is not strictly one-way: 'reconsolidation' shows that recalling a memory can make it temporarily editable again before it re-stabilizes — so memories can be updated, not just stored.

atoms.note: Complementary learning systems: a fast hippocampal learner trains a slow cortical learner via replay, avoiding catastrophic forgetting — an idea later borrowed into AI.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between synaptic consolidation and systems consolidation?
quiz.answer: Synaptic consolidation stabilizes individual synapses over hours via protein synthesis; systems consolidation reorganizes a memory over days–years from hippocampus-dependent to distributed neocortical storage.

quiz.prompt: Why is interleaved hippocampal replay during sleep useful for the cortex?
quiz.answer: Slow, interleaved replay trains the cortex gradually so new memories are integrated without overwriting old ones, avoiding catastrophic interference.

atoms.title: Attention & selective processing
atoms.summary: Limited processing resources are allocated to behaviorally relevant stimuli by enhancing some signals and suppressing others.

depths.eli5: Your brain can't fully process everything hitting your senses at once, so it picks. It turns up the 'volume' on whatever matters right now and turns down everything else. That selective spotlight is attention — and it's why you can hear one person at a noisy party.
depths.core: Attention comes in two flavors: bottom-up (grabbed automatically by something salient, like a sudden flash) and top-down (aimed on purpose by your goals). Its main neural signature is gain modulation — attended stimuli make sensory neurons fire more strongly and more reliably, while competing, ignored stimuli get suppressed (an idea called 'biased competition,' where stimuli compete and attention tips the balance). Control signals come from frontoparietal networks (regions across the frontal and parietal lobes). The measurable effects are stronger firing, sharper tuning (more selective responses), and less random trial-to-trial noise for the attended feature.
depths.deep: A leading mechanistic account is 'normalization-based': attention scales the gain inside a divisive-normalization circuit (one that divides each cell's response by the total activity of its neighbors), so whether attention looks like multiplying the response or just adding to it depends on the stimulus contrast and how big the stimulus is relative to the receptive field. Attention also tunes oscillatory coherence (for example, gamma-band synchrony between areas) to route information where it's needed. In effect attention is the gatekeeper deciding which representations reach the brain's capacity-limited stage — the same stage many theories tie to conscious awareness.

atoms.title: Perception as inference
atoms.summary: Perception is the brain's best guess about the world's causes given ambiguous sensory data — unconscious inference.

depths.eli5: Your eyes and ears never give you the full, clean truth — just partial, blurry, ambiguous clues. So your brain quietly fills in the most likely story behind those clues. In other words, what you 'see' is partly an educated guess. That's exactly why optical illusions fool you: they're cases where the brain's best guess is wrong.
depths.core: Sensory input doesn't pin down the world uniquely — this is the 'inverse problem': many different real scenes can produce the very same image on your retina (for example, a small near object and a large far one). So the brain has to infer the likely cause using prior knowledge — what Hermann von Helmholtz called 'unconscious inference.' A striking demonstration is cue combination: when people judge something using both sight and touch, they weight each sense by how reliable it is, almost exactly as an ideal statistical observer would — evidence that the brain effectively computes with probabilities.
depths.deep: Formally, perception approximates Bayesian inference: you combine the 'likelihood' (how well the current sensory evidence fits each possible cause) with a 'prior' (your expectations and the statistics of natural scenes) to land on the most probable cause — the 'posterior.' Under this view, illusions, flip-flopping (bistable) percepts, and context effects aren't malfunctions; they're the fingerprints of priors and of competing hypotheses fighting it out. This 'Bayesian brain' framing is the bridge from earlier atoms (receptive fields, population codes) to predictive coding and to theories of what we consciously experience.

atoms.note: Optimal cue combination: the brain weights each sense by its reliability (its inverse variance) — measurable evidence that perception is probabilistic.

atoms.title: Neural oscillations & synchrony
atoms.summary: Coordinated rhythmic activity across populations organizes timing, communication, and plasticity in the brain.

depths.eli5: Large groups of neurons often fall into a shared rhythm, the way a crowd ends up clapping in time. These brain rhythms (you may have heard them called 'brain waves') help different parts of the brain talk to each other at just the right moments, like two people timing their words to a beat.
depths.core: Brain rhythms come in frequency bands with Greek-letter names — delta (slowest), theta, alpha, beta, gamma (fastest) — measured in cycles per second (hertz, Hz). They're generated mostly by the back-and-forth between excitatory cells and fast inhibitory interneurons (often coupled by gap junctions). These oscillations act like reference clocks: they open recurring 'windows' when cells are most excitable, organize when spikes occur (for example, theta-phase coding in the hippocampus, where a spike's timing within the theta rhythm carries information), and may route signals by lining up the rhythms of two communicating areas — an idea called 'communication through coherence.'
depths.deep: Gamma rhythms (roughly 30–80 Hz) usually arise from excitatory–inhibitory or inhibitory–inhibitory loops with a built-in feedback delay that sets the frequency. 'Cross-frequency coupling' — for instance, fast gamma bursts riding on the phase of slower theta waves — can pack several working-memory items into one rhythm at once (multiplexing). Because the phase of an oscillation controls when spikes land, it also gates the spike coincidences that drive STDP, tying network rhythms back to synaptic learning. A live debate remains: whether oscillations actively cause computation, or are just a side effect of balanced excitation/inhibition dynamics.

atoms.title: Neuromodulation & global brain states
atoms.summary: Diffuse systems (dopamine, acetylcholine, serotonin, norepinephrine) reconfigure whole networks, signaling reward, arousal, and uncertainty.

depths.eli5: A handful of small clusters of neurons spray special chemicals broadly across the whole brain, changing its overall mood and mode all at once — alert versus drowsy, learning versus ignoring, exploring something new versus sticking with what works. These chemicals are called neuromodulators because they 'modulate' (adjust) how everything else behaves.
depths.core: Neuromodulators are released from small nuclei (compact clusters of neurons) but broadcast widely instead of point-to-point. They act mostly through slow metabotropic receptors (the G-protein kind from earlier) to adjust gain, excitability, and plasticity — they retune circuits rather than carrying fast specific messages. Dopamine neurons signal a 'reward prediction error': a burst when things turn out better than expected, a dip when worse. Acetylcholine and norepinephrine set arousal and flag how much uncertainty is expected versus surprising. Serotonin shapes mood, patience, and how fast you learn.
depths.deep: Dopamine's reward-prediction-error signal (characterized by Wolfram Schultz) closely matches the 'temporal-difference error' from reinforcement learning theory — making it the clearest known case of a brain signal implementing a specific learning algorithm, and a direct bridge to model-free reinforcement learning in AI. More broadly, neuromodulators act like the brain's 'hyperparameters' (the high-level settings of a learning system): they tune learning rate, the balance between exploring and exploiting, and the signal-to-noise ratio, switching the brain between whole-body modes like attentive learning, memory replay, and sleep.

atoms.title: Integrate-and-fire neuron models
atoms.equation: \tau_m\frac{dV}{dt} = -(V-V_{rest}) + R\,I(t),\quad \text{spike if } V \geq V_{th}\to V\leftarrow V_{reset}
atoms.summary: A minimal spiking model that keeps the essence — integrate inputs, fire at threshold, reset — while discarding channel detail.

depths.eli5: Here's a stripped-down toy version of a neuron: picture a leaky cup slowly filling with water. Inputs pour water in; the leak drains some out. When the water rises to the brim, the cup tips over (that's the 'spike'), empties, and starts again. It ignores almost all the biological detail, yet it captures the one thing that matters — when the neuron fires.
depths.core: The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model treats the membrane as a simple RC circuit (resistor + capacitor): it adds up (integrates) incoming current toward a steady value, leaks it away with time constant τ_m, and the instant the voltage V reaches a threshold V_th it emits a spike and snaps back to a reset value. It deliberately throws away the detailed shape of the spike (which carries no information, since every spike is identical) but keeps the two essentials — building up below threshold and the threshold crossing. That makes LIF simple enough to analyze with pen and paper and cheap enough to simulate in huge networks.
depths.deep: LIF is the workhorse of computational neuroscience: it yields clean closed-form 'f–I curves' (firing rate as a function of input current), supports the analysis of balanced networks and their irregular firing, and underpins spiking neural network models and energy-efficient 'neuromorphic' chips (hardware built to mimic neurons). Cheap extensions — the adaptive exponential and Izhikevich models — add features like firing-rate adaptation and bursting, recovering much of the Hodgkin–Huxley richness without tracking every channel. LIF is the right level of abstraction for asking network-scale questions where individual channel kinetics don't matter.

atoms.note: The spike waveform is stereotyped and carries no information, so LIF deletes it and keeps only its timing — exactly the right thing to abstract away.

atoms.title: Neurons as dynamical systems
atoms.summary: The diversity of firing patterns — tonic, bursting, resonating — emerges from the bifurcation structure of a neuron's nonlinear dynamics.

depths.eli5: Real neurons do more than the leaky-bucket picture suggests. Some fire at a steady drumbeat, some fire in bursts (clusters of spikes), and some only respond to inputs arriving at a particular rhythm. Where do these different behaviors come from? From the math of how a neuron's internal state tips over from 'quiet' to 'spiking' — the study of which is called dynamical systems.
depths.core: Treating a neuron as a 'dynamical system' (a system described by a few variables that evolve over time according to rules) explains its whole repertoire of firing patterns from just a couple of variables. The switch from rest to repetitive firing happens at a 'bifurcation' — a tipping point where a tiny change in input qualitatively changes the behavior. Which type of bifurcation a neuron has sets its 'excitability class': integrators (a 'saddle-node' bifurcation) can start firing at arbitrarily slow rates and simply sum inputs, while resonators (a 'Hopf' bifurcation) have a preferred input frequency and a minimum firing rate they jump to. Compact models like Eugene Izhikevich's two-variable equations reproduce most known cortical firing types for about the computational cost of one integrate-and-fire neuron.
depths.deep: This dynamical-systems view (built on classic reduced models like FitzHugh–Nagumo and Izhikevich) replaces labeling cell types with explaining mechanism. Bursting comes from a fast spike-generating subsystem being slowly switched on and off by a slower variable. Resonance and subthreshold oscillations turn some neurons into band-pass filters in time, biasing them toward inputs at certain rhythms — and toward STDP at those frequencies. The same lens scales up to whole networks, which have their own attractors (stable states), limit cycles (stable rhythms), and bifurcations — making low-dimensional dynamics, rather than single spikes, the natural language for describing cortical computation.

atoms.note: Integrator (saddle-node, can fire from near 0 Hz) vs resonator (Hopf, has a preferred frequency) — the bifurcation type, not the cell-type label, predicts the behavior.

atoms.title: The perceptron
atoms.summary: A neuron abstracted to a thresholded weighted sum — the foundational unit of artificial neural networks, with a provable learning rule.

depths.eli5: Strip a neuron down to its essential job and you get a 'perceptron.' It takes several inputs, multiplies each one by a number saying how important it is (a 'weight'), adds them all up, and fires a 1 if the total beats a threshold (otherwise a 0). Show it examples and let it nudge its weights every time it guesses wrong, and it gradually learns to sort simple categories. This little unit is the seed of modern AI.
depths.core: Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958) abstracts a neuron as y = Θ(Σ wᵢxᵢ − b): a weighted sum of the inputs xᵢ (each scaled by a weight wᵢ), shifted by a bias b, then passed through a step function Θ that outputs 1 if the result is positive and 0 otherwise. The 'perceptron learning rule' adjusts the weights toward any example it got wrong — a supervised (answer-key-using) cousin of Hebbian learning. The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees it will find a dividing line that separates the two classes IF such a straight line exists (the data are 'linearly separable'). It is the direct ancestor of every artificial neural network.
depths.deep: A single perceptron can only compute 'linearly separable' functions — ones you can split with a straight line (or flat plane). Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert famously showed it can't compute XOR (output 1 only when exactly one of two inputs is on), a limitation that stalled the whole field until multilayer networks trained by backpropagation overcame it. The lineage is explicit: the perceptron's weighted-sum-and-threshold is the earlier McCulloch–Pitts neuron and biological synaptic integration, abstracted; stack many of them and train by gradient descent (nudging weights downhill on the error) and you get deep learning. The biological caveat: backpropagation needs to send error signals backward through the exact forward weights, which is not obviously something local synapses (Hebb/STDP) can do — a central open question linking AI back to the brain.

atoms.note: One perceptron can't compute XOR (Minsky–Papert); you need a hidden layer. That gap is exactly why network depth matters.

atoms.title: From neurons to artificial neural networks
atoms.summary: Deep networks stack simple neuron-like units into trainable hierarchies, mirroring (and diverging from) cortical processing.

depths.eli5: Take that simple perceptron unit, wire thousands of them together in layers (the output of one layer feeds the next), and train the whole stack to turn inputs into the right outputs. This echoes how the brain builds simple features into complex ones, layer by layer — but the way these networks actually learn is quite different from the brain.
depths.core: Artificial neural networks stack layers of units, each doing a weighted sum followed by a nonlinearity (a simple bending function so the network can represent more than straight lines). They learn their weights by gradient descent (adjust every weight a little to reduce the error) using backpropagation (an efficient way to compute how much each weight contributed to the error by passing it backward through the layers). Convolutional networks borrowed the brain's receptive-field hierarchy directly — local filters plus pooling, echoing simple and complex cells. Remarkably, trained deep networks predict the responses of real visual-cortex neurons (from V1 up to IT) better than hand-designed models do — a striking overlap between machine and brain representations.
depths.deep: But the convergence is only partial. The brain learns largely without labeled answer keys, leans heavily on local plasticity (Hebb/STDP) and on recurrence and feedback, and is vastly more energy-efficient. Standard deep networks instead use global, non-local backpropagation and supervised targets. Closing this gap — finding biologically plausible 'credit assignment' (how each synapse learns its share of the blame for an error), via ideas like feedback alignment, predictive coding as an approximation to backpropagation, and equilibrium propagation — is an active frontier where neuroscience and AI feed each other directly.

atoms.note: Trained convolutional nets predict ventral-stream neural responses surprisingly well — yet they rely on non-local backprop, unlike the brain's local Hebbian/STDP rules.

atoms.title: Predictive coding & the free-energy principle
atoms.summary: The cortex may work by predicting its own inputs top-down and propagating only the prediction errors upward, minimizing surprise.

depths.eli5: Here's a bold idea about how the brain works: instead of shipping raw sense data upward, each level of the brain guesses what it expects to sense, and only the differences from that guess — the surprises — get passed along. Learning then means improving the guesses so there are fewer and fewer surprises. It's an efficient way to run a brain: don't report what you already predicted, only report the news.
depths.core: Predictive coding (Rajesh Rao & Dana Ballard, 1999) proposes a hierarchy in which each level sends top-down predictions to the level below, and the lower level sends back only the 'prediction error' — the leftover part its prediction missed. Perception is the process of settling into a state that minimizes those errors; learning slowly adjusts the internal 'generative model' that produces the predictions. Karl Friston's free-energy principle generalizes this: the brain acts to minimize a quantity called variational free energy, a mathematical upper bound on 'surprise.' That single objective covers both perception (update your beliefs to fit the input) and action (change the input to fit your beliefs by moving your body).
depths.deep: Mechanistically the theory predicts two kinds of units in the cortex: prediction units (proposed to live in deep cortical layers) and error units (in superficial layers). A key knob is 'precision' — how reliable an error is judged to be, plausibly set by neuromodulatory gain — which weights how much each error counts; this is how the framework reinterprets attention (paying attention = boosting the precision of certain errors). Under simplifying (linear-Gaussian) assumptions, predictive-coding updates approximate backpropagation, offering a biologically local route to gradient-style learning. The framework is ambitious and contested, with active debate over what would count as evidence for or against it.

atoms.note: Precision-weighting of prediction errors is how this framework reinterprets attention; under certain assumptions its updates approximate backpropagation locally.
